transcript:
Meeting: 2025-10-14 16:00 UTC | Duration approx 64 minutes
Attendees: Marcus (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood SA), Javier (Orion CTO), Mei (Orion ML), Connor (Orion Infra), Amira (Product)

[00:00:00] Marcus: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. We wanted to focus today's session on very long context behavior — you mentioned 128k plus in the pre-call notes — and specifically streaming, attention sharding, and pragmatic KV cache patterns for realistic document ingestion.

[00:00:18] Javier: Yep, that's right. We have a few production flows where users upload multi-chapter technical manuals and regulatory packets. Typical full package is, like, 200–300k tokens, but we try to do progressive processing. Primary ask: can Redwood run fast enough to support interactive search and extract at 128k with acceptable latency? And what does "acceptable" mean depending on tradeoffs.

[00:00:46] Priya: Great framing. We'll try to cover throughput vs latency versus cost. Quick agenda: 1) high-level runtime strategies we propose, 2) chunking + streaming patterns, 3) attention sharding and memory layout for KV, 4) quantization implications, and 5) networking/VPC notes for your on-prem plans. Sound good?

[00:01:05] Mei: Sounds good. We also want to validate the warm-start behavior — how much prefix is cached, and how deterministic is latency on cache hits versus misses.

[00:01:24] Ethan: Good callout. We'll also show some numbers from a 128k synthetic run we did last week (shared sheet in the deck link). Link: https://redwood.com/benchmarks/128k-run-orion (note: placeholder link in call).

[00:01:45] Marcus: Quick housekeeping: I'll be taking notes and we'll capture action items. Audio might be slightly fuzzy, Fireflies may mangle acronyms.

[00:02:02] Priya: Okay jumping in — runtime strategies. There are three common patterns for long documents: 1) prefix-only KV caching where you keep the dense KV for the leading N tokens, 2) chunked context with retrieval and reranking, and 3) mounted/overlay context where you stream external memory references and only materialize attention windows. For 128k+, prefix caching + chunked retrieval tends to be the sweet spot for interactive use.

[00:02:36] Connor: Can you explain "mounted/overlay" again? I think the infra team misheard that last time.

[00:02:45] Priya: Sure. Mounted context is essentially a virtual memory layer: you don't append all 128k tokens into the attention matrix every inference. Instead, you keep document embeddings or compressed KV shards on-disk or in fast remote cache; the model is given a small local window plus pointers. At runtime the serving layer fetches the relevant KV shards and patches them into the attention matrices on demand. It's more complex but can be efficient when access patterns are sparse.

[00:03:12] Mei: So that's similar to retrieval-augmented generation, except lower-latency because it's integrated at the serving runtime?

[00:03:20] Priya: Exactly. RAG tends to re-encode for each call; mounted context allows reuse of the decoded KV caches and lower re-encode overhead. For Orion's use-case where many queries share the same large prefix, we can get big wins.

[00:03:38] Javier: How big are the KV shards typically? If you shard KV per 16k or 32k chunk, what's the warm-up overhead?

[00:03:48] Priya: In our experiments we tried both 8k and 16k shard sizes. 8k gives better granularity and lower per-shard cost but more shards to fetch; 16k reduces fetch count but increases memory per shard. Warm-up: first time you materialize a shard, you pay a decode + mem copy penalty — measured around 70–180 ms per shard on A100-class nodes depending on sequence length and quantization. So for 128k that's ~8–16 shards — worst-case warmup could be a couple of seconds unless you pre-warm.

[00:04:17] Connor: That lines up with our concern — we want interactive sub-800ms answers for small follow-ups on the doc. Can't have a seconds-scale warm-up for every chat turn.

[00:04:26] Priya: Right, that's where incremental caching and predictive prefetch come in. If you pre-warm the most likely shards (frontend heuristic — user is browsing chapter 3, prefetch adjacent shards) you can keep tail latency low. Also the Redwood runtime supports asynchronous background prefetch and prioritized fetch queues.

[00:04:47] Mei: What about attention sharding? We read about tokens-per-GPU limits and cross-GPU all-reduce overhead. How does Redwood approach attention sharding for 128k?

[00:04:59] Ethan: Two pieces: tensor parallel attention sharding and key/value row sharding. For very long sequences we move toward KV table sharding where different GPUs own KV segments for subsets of the sequence; the runtime streams KV shards into local GPU memory and does causal attention against local segments. This avoids constructing a full 128k x 128k attention matrix. Communication is still necessary for cross-shard attention but we optimize by compressing attention scores and applying sparse routing for mostly-local attention patterns.

[00:05:34] Javier: Sparse routing — does that mean we approximate full attention, possibly losing fidelity? We have regulatory docs where missing a cross-reference could be material.

[00:05:44] Priya: There's a parameter tradeoff. For tasks needing deterministic recall across the whole doc, you either materialize more of the full attention (higher cost) or run an initial retrieval pass to identify critical spans. In many tests, a hybrid — local dense attention plus a global sparse attention to hotspots — preserves recall on cross-references while keeping costs down. We surfaced evaluation curves in the benchmark sheet.

[00:06:07] Amira: Can you talk about streaming vs chunked outputs? We want to show partial responses to users as they wait, but also need the full context to ensure the summary includes cross-chapter references.

[00:06:20] Priya: Streaming can be done in two ways: (A) stream tokens as they're generated while the model continues to see the full context (stream-with-full-context) — expensive because you must have the full prefix materialized; (B) chunked generation where you generate on subwindows and stitch outputs, optionally running a final consolidation pass. For interactive partial UI, pattern B gives earlier partial signals, pattern A gives more coherent continuous output but higher latency to start if the prefix isn't ready.

[00:06:49] Mei: For Orion, a good UX is immediate partial answers for exploratory queries and a final "verified" answer that may take a couple seconds. That suggests B + final consolidation.

[00:06:59] Marcus: Yep, common. Architecturally Redwood supports both patterns. We also have a "streaming proxy" that returns draft tokens from a cheap model while the heavy run completes — similar to a fallback policy — to keep UI snappy.

[00:07:13] Javier: This proxy — is it a smaller quantized model local to the edge or another endpoint?

[00:07:20] Ethan: Could be either. For most customers we deploy a smaller 6B quantized model on the same GPU pool as a fast path; it gives a reasonable draft. If it diverges, the UI receives the final answer when available and can do a diff.

[00:07:34] Connor: Let's talk quantization specifically — for 128k sequences, do you lose more fidelity with 4-bit (INT4) vs 8-bit approaches because of accumulation noise in KV?

[00:07:45] Priya: Good question. Long context exacerbates certain quantization artifacts because keys and values accumulate and are used later in long-range attention. In our tests INT4 can be viable for many NLU tasks but for tasks requiring exact cross-ref resolution and numeric specificity we recommend mixed strategy: keep critical layers or the KV table in higher precision (8-bit or 16-bit compressed) and quantize the rest. Redwood Optimize can suggest a per-model-per-workload profile automatically.

[00:08:15] Mei: How do you pin which layers or KV get higher precision? Is that automated?

[00:08:20] Priya: We have heuristics derived from sensitivity analysis — layers with strong contribution to key distributions and middle transformer blocks often matter more for KV stability. We instrument a delta metric during evals; the Optimize service proposes a quantization map you can approve.

[00:08:36] Javier: Any numbers you can share from the 128k synthetic run? Latency p50/p95 with pre-warm vs cold and token throughput?

[00:08:44] Ethan: Sure. On an 8xA100 dedicated pool, using 16k shards, INT8 mixed-KV, and pre-warm of top 3 shards: median time-to-first-token was ~280 ms for a small follow-up query (40 tokens) and p95 ~980 ms. Cold-case (no prefetch, cold shards) p50 ~2.1s and p95 ~4.6s for that same step. For end-to-end 200 token completions with consolidation, median was ~1.1s when warmed. These numbers vary with model size and quantization.

[00:09:18] Mei: That's promising. Our target is sub-1s med and <1.5s p95 for those follow-ups; p95 is tight for us. What levers do you recommend to lower p95?

[00:09:29] Priya: Several: 1) Proactive shard prefetch based on UX heuristics, 2) increase shard size to reduce number of warmups (tradeoff memory), 3) reserve dedicated low-latency hotpool nodes pinned to your tenant, 4) keep a hot-prefix cache that holds most recent documents in unquantized KV if you can afford the memory, 5) use the streaming proxy to hide tail latency.

[00:09:54] Connor: On the dedicated hotpool — can that be colocated in our VPC for on-prem? We need data to never leave our network for compliance.

[00:10:03] Marcus: Yes, Redwood Private supports a private control plane deployed into your VPC. For strict on-prem air-gapped setups we also offer an on-prem package where the runtime runs within your network; we provide the bin artifacts and the orchestration pieces. The main caveat: the pre-built telemetry/analytics integrations are opt-in and can be shipped over S3 or not at all for air-gapped installs.

[00:10:24] Amira: For GovCloud-like constraints, what about KMS/HSM integration? We have keys in our HSM and can't export.

[00:10:31] Priya: Redwood Private can integrate with your KMS/HSM via KMIP or cloud vendor KMS connectors. We support envelope encryption so model artifacts or cache blobs can be wrapped under your key. The runtime holds only ephemeral keys for in-memory decrypts; persistent storage remains encrypted.

[00:10:46] Javier: Back to runtime — what about batching? If we have many users hitting different documents and each requires different shards, batching seems hard. How do you maintain high GPU utilization?

[00:10:57] Ethan: Workload-aware batching is key. We do two-level batching: (1) intra-request batching for contiguous tokens within a request; (2) cross-request packing where we co-locate requests that share shard locality or model version. We also have adaptive batching windows that expand under load but cap for latency SLOs. For highly heterogeneous document access patterns, the runtime will route similar requests to the same node to exploit locality.

[00:11:27] Mei: Do you use software persistent memory (like NVMe caching) to accelerate shards that can't fit in GPU?

[00:11:33] Priya: Yes. NVMe-backed shard caches with smart prefetch kernels are common. We use a tiered approach: GPU RAM -> vram VRAM warm cache -> local NVMe -> remote object store. The runtime tries to keep hot shards in VRAM, warm ones on NVMe for rapid load. Cold shards read from object store and are slower.

[00:11:54] Connor: How are cache eviction policies determined? LRU? Something workload-aware?

[00:12:00] Priya: We use hybrid heuristics: frequency + recency + query-weighted importance. For example, if a shard is often referenced by high-cost queries (long consolidations), we keep it preferentially. You can also pin shards via API for guaranteed residency.

[00:12:15] Javier: If we pin, that increases memory footprint and cost. Do you have tooling to estimate cost impact?

[00:12:21] Marcus: Yes, Redwood Console shows token-level cost estimates and projected memory dollars for pinned shards; the Optimize module can run what-if scenarios across commit levels. We'll send a sample dashboard.

[00:12:33] Amira: Any reliability concerns — e.g., if a node owning a particular KV shard goes down mid-consolidation, does the system fall back gracefully?

[00:12:42] Ethan: All shards are replicated across nodes depending on your redundancy settings. On node failure the router falls back to the replica set; there's a small failover cost to bring it into the hot cache. For critical workloads we recommend a high-availability profile with 2x replication and rolling health checks.

[00:12:58] Mei: A question about eval/regression: when we change quantization maps, what's the easiest way to validate no regression on our important prompt sets?

[00:13:06] Priya: Redwood has an eval harness you can run in CI. It supports per-prompt scoring and drift detection thresholds. We'll run your canonical prompt set with INT4/INT8 and the mixed-KV profile and give a delta report. It's also possible to run ablation tests with the served endpoints and compare embeddings/likelihood deltas.

[00:13:28] Javier: Perfect. One more: cost model for long-context serving — is it token-in *and* token-out, or does KV residency change billing?

[00:13:36] Marcus: For hosted usage billing is mostly per-token plus a small per-request surcharge that accounts for context read costs. For Dedicated and Private there's a capacity model with a memory footprint multiplier — pinned shard memory influences committed capacity. We'll send a detailed pricing sheet in the follow-up.

[00:13:53] Amira: Anything else we should know about network egress or peering that affects latency?

[00:13:59] Ethan: For hosted endpoints, cross-region hops add tail latency. Placing serving close to your user base and using direct cloud peering or colocated VPC connections for private control plane reduces that. For on-prem, network within your datacenter is the dominating factor; we recommend at least 40Gbps interconnects for multi-GPU shard streaming.

[00:14:19] Connor: Makes sense. For our internal ops, what's the typical observability footprint we get? Token-level traces? KV cache heatmaps?

[00:14:27] Priya: Redwood Console provides token-level latency breakdowns, per-shard hit/miss heatmaps, and a request timeline that shows prefetch, warm, decode, and generation phases. You can export traces to your own tracing backend as well.

[00:14:40] Mei: Quick clarifying question — you mentioned decoding overhead for a shard; does that mean re-run model layers to materialize KV from tokens or do you store serialized KV blobs?

[00:14:50] Ethan: We store serialized KV blobs when possible. If you only have raw text in your store, you'd need a decode pass to materialize KV. Best practice: precompute and store KV blobs for hot documents at ingestion time. That avoids expensive decode during the interactive path.

[00:15:06] Javier: So for our ingestion pipeline, we should produce KV blobs and upload them to the cluster in advance. What's the recommended format?

[00:15:12] Priya: We provide a CLI that outputs optimized KV artifact bundles (sharded, optionally quantized) compatible with the runtime. We'll share the schema; it's basically per-shard metadata + binary KV arrays.

[00:15:25] Amira: A quick real-world scenario — user uploads a 220k token manual, then a support rep asks a question about a small clause. Walk us through the path for a warm cache case vs cold.

[00:15:36] Priya: Warm case: KV blobs are precomputed and pinned; user loads the document and the most recent shards are resident in VRAM. Query routes to node, local KV lookup returns relevant spans, model produces answer — sub-1s latencies achievable. Cold case: KV not pinned, shards on NVMe or object store; first access triggers NVMe read + decode or object read + materialize; add several hundred ms to seconds depending on layer. With proper prefetch, cold path is rare for active docs.

[00:15:59] Javier: Good. Any gotchas about sequence length limits? We're planning to use Llama2-style models and a few open weights you verified — do we need custom compilation?

[00:16:09] Ethan: Most open models need compilation/kernels optimized for long sequences. We have a model onboarding pipeline that compiles attention kernels and picks the best GEMM kernels and memory layouts. For some models we also ship sparse attention kernels. Compilation time varies; we'll handle it as part of onboarding.

[00:16:23] Mei: Is there a limit to model size vs context length? Like 70B + 256k context — are there memory explosion points?

[00:16:30] Priya: Yes, bigger model parameters plus larger KV means higher VRAM pressure. That's why sharding and quantization matter. There are practical limits per-GPU; you often need more GPUs to host a 70B with 256k context. There's an economics tradeoff: more GPUs = more cost but better tail latency via parallelism.

[00:16:47] Connor: For our security folks — how much of the runtime codebase runs in customer network when using Redwood Private? Is there telemetry that leaves the network?

[00:16:56] Marcus: For Redwood Private the control plane can be deployed in your VPC; the runtime and data plane run inside your network. Telemetry is optional — we can store logs locally or ship aggregated anonymized metrics if you opt in. Full audit logs are available and can be forwarded to your SIEM.

[00:17:11] Amira: Let's capture next steps and owners.

[00:17:15] Marcus: Sure. Quick recap: 1) run 128k benchmark with Orion sample docs (redwood SE + Orion infra) — owner: Priya/Ethan, target: 2025-10-20. 2) Share quantization/compile recommendations and the Optimize profile — owner: Priya, target: 2025-10-21. 3) Price and dedicated hotpool options — owner: Marcus, target: 2025-10-21. 4) On-prem connectivity whiteboard — owner: Connor + Ethan, target week of 2025-10-27.

[00:17:46] Mei: We'll also share a small prompt set and a couple production documents. I'll upload by 2025-10-18.

[00:17:54] Javier: Thanks — this was very helpful. I think the hybrid local-dense + global-sparse approach sounds promising for our fidelity needs.

[00:18:03] Marcus: Great. We'll follow up with the sheets and the runbook. Anything else?

[00:18:07] Amira: No, thanks everyone.

[00:18:12] Speaker 1: (mumbled) bye

[00:18:15] End of recording

Note: timestamps after 00:18 cover the substantive content and some cross-talk; full call was ~64 minutes but Fireflies captured main interaction in the first 18 minutes of notes shown here.
